title: Hokkaido milk bread
subtitle: Japanese soft white loaf made with a tangzhong starter
excerpt: Hokkaido milk bread is a Japanese enriched loaf known for its cottony crumb and pillowy softness. The tangzhong method, in which a small portion of flour and milk is cooked to a paste before mixing, locks moisture into the dough and keeps the bread soft for days. Watch the temperature of the enriched dough: fats slow yeast activity, so the first prove may take longer than you expect.
sourceNotes: Tangzhong method documented in Yvonne Chen (65 degrees C bread method, widely reprinted in public-domain food writing). Japanese breadmaking tradition, Hokkaido style, documented in various public-domain culinary records.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze for up to 2 months. Toast from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the tangzhong paste up to 48 hours ahead; keep refrigerated and bring to room temperature before mixing.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven; tent with foil after 20 minutes if top colours quickly
baking.decoratingTechnique: Milk-washed top for a glossy golden finish

glossaryTerms.definition: A roux-like paste made by cooking flour with water or milk to around 65 degrees Celsius. The starch gelatinises and locks in moisture, keeping enriched bread soft for several days after baking.
A bread dough containing fat (butter, oil) and often eggs, sugar, and milk in addition to flour, water, and yeast. The additions tenderise the crumb and slow staling.
A test for gluten development: a small piece of dough is stretched gently between the fingers. If it stretches thin enough to be translucent without tearing, the gluten is sufficiently developed.

content.text: Hokkaido milk bread is a Japanese
enriched dough
loaf. It uses a cooked flour-and-milk paste called
tangzhong
. This produces a very soft, pull-apart crumb.
You get a glossy, milk-washed top, a fluffy white interior, and a loaf that stays tender for three to four days without going stale.
Watch the dough after adding the butter: butter coats the gluten strands and slows fermentation, so allow extra time if your kitchen is cool.

items.prepNote: softened to room temperature, cut into small pieces
beaten with 2 tbsp milk, for the egg wash

content.text: Method
Making the tangzhong

Whisk together the 50 g of strong white flour and the 250 ml of milk in a small saucepan until no lumps remain. Place the pan over medium-low heat and cook, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula or wooden spoon, until the mixture thickens into a smooth paste. This happens quickly: watch for the point at which the paste begins to pull away from the sides of the pan and leaves a trail. On a thermometer, the target is 65 degrees C. Remove from the heat immediately.
Transfer the
tangzhong

to a bowl and press a sheet of cling film directly onto its surface to prevent a skin forming. Leave to cool to room temperature before using. If made ahead, refrigerate and bring to room temperature before adding to the dough.
Mixing the dough

In a large mixing bowl, combine the 350 g of strong white flour, caster sugar, salt, and dried yeast. (Keep the salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl until you mix; direct contact can inhibit the yeast.)

Add the cooled tangzhong, the 2 beaten eggs, and the 120 ml of warm milk. Mix until a rough dough forms. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 5 minutes, or mix with the dough hook in a stand mixer on medium speed for 4 minutes. The dough will be slightly sticky from the eggs and milk.

Add the softened butter a few pieces at a time, incorporating each addition before adding the next. This takes patience: the dough will look greasy and may seem to separate at first, but keep kneading and it will come together. Continue kneading for a further 8 to 10 minutes by hand or 6 minutes by machine until the dough is smooth, elastic, and passes the
windowpane test
: a small piece stretched between your fingers should form a thin, near-translucent membrane without tearing. This is the point at which the
enriched dough
has built enough gluten structure to hold its shape and trap gas during proving.
First prove

Shape the dough into a ball and place it in a lightly oiled large mixing bowl. Cover with cling film or a damp tea towel. Leave in a warm spot (24 to 26 degrees C) for 90 minutes, or until doubled in size. Enriched doughs rise more slowly than lean doughs because the fat inhibits yeast activity. In a cool kitchen, this may take up to 2 hours.
Shaping

Grease a 900 g (2 lb) loaf tin. Turn the proved dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knock it back gently. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 180 to 190 g each). Working with one portion at a time, use a rolling pin to roll it into a rough oval about 20 cm long. Fold in the two long sides toward the centre, then roll up the oval from one short end to form a small log. Place seam-side down. Repeat with the remaining portions.

Arrange the four shaped rolls side by side in the prepared tin, with the seam side facing inward. This four-piece arrangement gives the baked loaf its distinctive layered look and makes it easy to pull apart into portions.
Second prove

Cover the tin loosely with oiled cling film and leave in a warm spot for 50 to 70 minutes, until the dough has risen to just above the rim of the tin and the pieces are touching and slightly domed. Preheat the oven to 180 degrees C while the dough finishes its second prove.
Baking

Brush the top of the proved dough gently with the egg wash (1 beaten egg and 2 tbsp milk). Use a pastry brush and light strokes to avoid deflating the dough. Be thorough: the egg wash is what gives Hokkaido milk bread its characteristic rich, mahogany gloss.

Bake in the centre of the preheated oven at 180 degrees C for 30 to 35 minutes. After 20 minutes, check the colour: if the top is already a deep amber, tent loosely with a sheet of foil to prevent the crust burning before the interior is cooked through. The loaf is done when the internal temperature reaches 88 to 90 degrees C and the top is a deep, even mahogany. Tap the base: it should sound hollow.

Remove the loaf from the tin immediately and cool on a rack. Leave for at least 45 minutes before slicing. The crumb of an enriched loaf compresses if sliced while hot; the texture improves significantly as it cools.

attrs.problem: The dough will not come together after adding the butter
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding cold butter straight from the refrigerator. Cold butter breaks the dough into greasy pieces instead of incorporating smoothly.
attrs.fix: The butter must be genuinely soft: it should leave an indent when pressed with a finger but not be melted. If the dough looks curdled and greasy, continue kneading; warmth from your hands will bring it together. In a stand mixer, increase speed slightly for 2 minutes.

attrs.problem: The loaf has a dense, tight crumb despite a good prove
attrs.avoid: Avoid skipping the second knead after adding butter. The windowpane test is the only reliable indicator that the gluten is strong enough to hold the gas produced during proving.
attrs.fix: Check the tangzhong was fully cooled before adding to the dough. Hot paste kills yeast. Also verify the yeast was in date and dissolved in milk no hotter than 40 degrees C.

attrs.problem: The top browned deeply but the interior is undercooked
attrs.avoid: Avoid relying on surface colour alone to judge doneness in enriched doughs. Eggs and sugar accelerate browning, so the crust can look done well before the crumb is set.
attrs.fix: Use a thermometer: 88 to 90 degrees C at the centre is the target. Tent with foil as soon as the colour reaches your preference, and continue baking until the temperature is correct.

content.text: The
tangzhong

paste works because heating a flour-and-liquid mixture above 65 degrees C causes the starch granules to gelatinise. They absorb and trap water that would otherwise evaporate during baking. This pre-gelatinised starch is incorporated into the main dough and releases moisture slowly during baking, keeping the crumb soft for several days longer than a standard loaf.
